Greenland.text: The US secretly tried to build nuclear missile sites under its ice cap; Denmark, which it belongs to, found out in 1997.
Greenland.evidence: The United States tried to construct a subterranean network of secret nuclear missile launch sites in the Greenlandic ice cap, named Project Iceworm. ... The Danish government was not aware of the programme's mission until 1997, when they discovered it while looking in the declassified documents for records related to the crash of a nuclear-equipped B-52 bomber near the Thule air base in 1968.

New Guinea.text: Split between Indonesia and Papua New Guinea, its Fly River alone carries more water than all of Australia's rivers.
New Guinea.evidence: It has been estimated that the island's rivers carry about 1,500 km3/a (48,000 m3/s) of water into the sea, with Fly alone carrying more water (238 km3/a (7,500 m3/s)) than all the rivers in Australia combined.

Borneo.text: Shared by Brunei, Indonesia and Malaysia, it has a cave with over three million bats and guano over 100 metres deep.
Borneo.evidence: In Sarawak, the Clearwater Cave has one of the world's longest underground rivers while Deer Cave is home to over three million bats, with guano accumulated to over 100 metres (330 ft) deep.

Madagascar.text: Africa's largest island, its name may come from Marco Polo mixing it up with Mogadishu, in Somalia.
Madagascar.evidence: Another hypothesis is that Madagascar is a corrupted transliteration of Mogadishu, the capital of Somalia and an important medieval Indian Ocean port. This would have resulted from the 13th-century Venetian explorer Marco Polo's confusion of the two locations in his memoirs, in which he mentions the land of Madageiscar to the south of Socotra.

Baffin Island.text: In Canada, its Mount Thor is said to have the greatest sheer vertical drop of any mountain on Earth.
Baffin Island.evidence: Mount Thor, with an elevation of 1,675 m (5,495 ft), is said to have the greatest purely vertical drop (a sheer cliff face) of any mountain on Earth, at 1,250 m (4,100 ft).

Sumatra.text: In Indonesia, it is home to Rafflesia arnoldii, the world's largest individual flower.
Sumatra.evidence: Unique species include the Sumatran pine which dominates the Sumatran tropical pine forests of the higher mountainsides in the north of the island and rainforest plants such as Rafflesia arnoldii (the world's largest individual flower), and the titan arum (the world's largest unbranched inflorescence).

Honshu.text: Japan's largest island; the 2011 earthquake shifted its northeast by as much as 5.3 metres.
Honshu.evidence: Mountainous and volcanic, Honshu experiences frequent earthquakes (such as the Great Kantō earthquake, which heavily damaged Tokyo in September 1923; and the earthquake of March 2011, which moved the northeastern part of the island by varying amounts of as much as 5.3 m (17 ft) while causing devastating tsunamis).

Victoria Island.text: In Canada, it contains the world's largest island within an island within an island.
Victoria Island.evidence: Victoria Island contains the world's largest island within an island within an island.

Great Britain.text: Home to England, Scotland and Wales; "Britain" may come from a Celtic word for "the painted ones" or "the tattooed folk".
Great Britain.evidence: The name Britain descends from the Latin name for Britain, Britannia or Brittānia, the land of the Britons. ... It is derived from the travel writings of Pytheas around 320 BC, which described various islands in the North Atlantic as far north as Thule (probably Norway). ... The term used by Pytheas may derive from a Celtic word meaning "the painted ones" or "the tattooed folk" in reference to body decorations.

Ellesmere Island.text: In Canada, more than fifty Norse artifacts, including pieces of chain mail, have been found at old Thule sites here.
Ellesmere Island.evidence: More than fifty Norse artifacts have been found in Thule archaeological sites on the Bache Peninsula, including pieces of chain mail.
